prompt.context: The CEO of a startup in a small village in Italy has hired McKinsey to help them decide how many trucks to lease. There are different models available, but the client has been told that they must maintain a consistent fleet — they can only lease one model type. This company provides local delivery of packages sent to the village through UPS next-day-delivery service. The company operates as follows: (i) they receive every package at 5pm from UPS, (ii) a group of people sorts the packages and (iii) loads them on trucks where they are stored overnight, and (iv) delivery begins at 9am and runs for 10 hours.
prompt.question: How would you suggest approaching the client's problem of deciding how many trucks to lease and which truck model to choose?

clarifying_info.q: How many packages does the company deliver per day?
How long does it take to deliver a single package?
clarifying_info.a: 8 minutes on average to deliver a single package and be ready for the next one.

clarifying_info.q: What is the average size of a package?
What truck models are available and at what cost?
clarifying_info.a: Truck A costs $150 per day, dimensions 3x4x5. Truck B costs $40 per day, dimensions 9x2x1. Truck C costs $130 per day, dimensions 6x8x10 (double the size of Truck A).

clarifying_info.q: Are driver costs, fuel, and other variable costs relevant?
clarifying_info.a: No — drivers, fuel, etc. are not considered and do not make a material difference to the analysis for simplicity.

clarifying_info.q: How many days per week does the company operate?

exhibits.title: Truck Models — Cost and Dimensions
exhibits.shows: A table listing three truck models (A, B, C) with their daily lease cost and cargo dimensions
exhibits.data: Truck A: $150/day, dimensions 3x4x5; Truck B: $40/day, dimensions 9x2x1; Truck C: $130/day, dimensions 6x8x10

framework: Determine the time constraint: calculate the minimum number of trucks needed to deliver all packages within the 10-hour delivery window
Determine the space constraint: calculate the minimum number of trucks needed to carry all packages given each truck model's cargo volume
Take the binding constraint (whichever requires more trucks) for each model
Calculate the total daily cost for each model (trucks needed x cost per day)
Select the model that minimizes total daily cost while meeting both constraints
Consider qualitative factors and future optionality

questions.prompt: How many trucks are required to deliver all 1,000 packages within the 10-hour delivery window?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate total delivery time needed and divide by available time per truck. 8 min/package x 1,000 packages = 8,000 minutes of total delivery time. Each truck delivers for 10 hours = 600 minutes. 8,000 / 600 = 13.3 trucks, so a minimum of 14 trucks are needed to meet the time constraint.

math.setup: Total delivery time = 8 min/package x 1,000 packages = 8,000 minutes. Available time per truck = 10 hours x 60 min/hour = 600 minutes. Trucks needed = 8,000 / 600
steps: 10 hours x 60 min = 600 minutes per truck

questions.prompt: For each truck model, how many trucks are needed to carry all 1,000 packages given the cargo volume?
questions.guidance: Candidate should compute each truck's cargo volume, then divide total package volume (1,000 x 1x1x1 = 1,000 cubic units) by cargo volume per truck. Round up to nearest whole number. Compare this space-constrained number to the time-constrained minimum (14) and take the higher of the two.

math.setup: Total package volume = 1,000 packages x 1x1x1 = 1,000 cubic units. Truck volume = product of three dimensions. Trucks needed (space) = 1,000 / truck volume, rounded up.
steps: Truck A volume = 3x4x5 = 60. Trucks needed = 1,000/60 = 16.67 → 17 trucks. Time constraint = 14. Binding = 17.
Truck B volume = 9x2x1 = 18. Trucks needed = 1,000/18 = 55.56 → 56 trucks. Time constraint = 14. Binding = 56.
Truck C volume = 6x8x10 = 480. Trucks needed = 1,000/480 = 2.08 → 3 trucks. Time constraint = 14. Binding = 14.
math.answer: Truck A: 17 trucks required; Truck B: 56 trucks required; Truck C: 14 trucks required (time-constrained)

questions.prompt: What is the total daily cost for each truck model, and which model should the client lease?
questions.guidance: Multiply the number of trucks required (binding constraint) by the daily cost per truck for each model. Compare and recommend the lowest-cost option. Truck C is lowest cost overall. Candidate should also note that Truck C leaves substantial unused cargo capacity (14 trucks x 480 cu = 6,720 cu vs. 1,000 needed), which creates future optionality.

math.setup: Total daily cost = trucks required (binding) x cost per truck per day
math.answer: Truck C at $1,820/day is the lowest-cost option

brainstorming.prompt: Six months have passed and the recommendation was successful. The CEO now wants to understand potential risks the business should be assessing going forward.

categories.name: Internal risks
ideas: Need for extra/backup drivers — employees getting sick reduces delivery capacity
Unionized drivers may shift labor costs up in the future
Trucks can break down causing late or missed deliveries — need spare capacity or contingency
Drivers speeding to meet delivery windows could generate fines above forecast
Sorting and loading operation efficiency could become a bottleneck as volume grows

categories.name: External risks
ideas: Single supplier dependency on UPS — the business is captive to UPS pricing and terms
Adoption of digital communication (e-mail) could reduce physical package volumes over time
Government regulation changes affecting last-mile delivery
New competition entering the village with no real barriers to entry, since UPS would partner with any carrier meeting service/cost metrics
No proprietary brand — UPS could switch to a competitor or launch its own last-mile operation
Macroeconomic downturn reducing consumer and business shipment volumes

recommendation: Lease 14 trucks of Model C at $130/day each, for a total cost of $1,820/day
Model C satisfies both the time constraint (14 trucks needed) and the space constraint (3 trucks needed, well within 14), at the lowest total daily cost among all three options
risks: Model C trucks carry far more volume than currently needed — excess capacity is idle cost if volume does not grow
Single-supplier reliance on UPS creates pricing and continuity risk
No barriers to competitive entry could erode market position
next_steps: Explore utilization of excess truck capacity for additional revenue streams (see profit-growth discussion)
Negotiate favorable multi-year lease terms for Model C given fleet size
Assess contingency plan for truck breakdowns to protect on-time delivery SLA
